title: Can a CPA Represent You Before the IRS? Rules and Form 2848
metaDescription: A CPA can represent a taxpayer before the IRS with unlimited rights under Circular 230, once authorized on Form 2848, covering audits, appeals, and collections.
h1: Can a CPA Represent a Taxpayer Before the IRS?
cardBlurb: A Certified Public Accountant holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS under Circular 230 once authorized on Form 2848, covering audits, collections, and appeals.
introText:
A Certified Public Accountant (CPA) can represent a taxpayer before the [Internal Revenue Service (IRS)](https://www.irs.gov) on any tax matter, provided the CPA is in good standing and properly authorized on IRS Form 2848. Along with attorneys and Enrolled Agents, CPAs hold unlimited practice rights under federal regulations.

That authority allows a CPA to communicate directly with IRS personnel, appear at examination meetings, negotiate payment arrangements, and take disputes before the [IRS Independent Office of Appeals](https://www.irs.gov/appeals). The taxpayer does not need to attend those proceedings when a CPA represents them.

A CPA cannot simply call the IRS or attend an audit on a taxpayer's behalf without written authorization. The representation relationship requires specific federal documentation before the agency will disclose confidential records or recognize the CPA's legal authority to act.

sections.heading: What Circular 230 Authorizes a CPA to Do
sections.body:
Under [Circular 230](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/circular-230-tax-professionals), a CPA who is duly qualified to practice in any U.S. state, territory, possession, commonwealth, or the District of Columbia holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS. This authorization applies as long as the CPA is not currently suspended or disbarred from practice before the agency. The IRS regulations grant identical practice rights to three professional credentials: CPAs, attorneys, and Enrolled Agents. While each professional group completes different education, licensing exams, and jurisdictional requirements, their scope of practice rights before the IRS does not differ. Any of the three can handle any taxpayer matter, regardless of who prepared the original tax return.

That unlimited authority stands in contrast to the restricted rules that govern unenrolled return preparers. The IRS outlines these distinctions in its guidance on [tax return preparer credentials and qualifications](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/understanding-tax-return-preparer-credentials-and-qualifications). An individual who participates in the IRS Annual Filing Season Program holds limited representation rights. Such a preparer may only represent taxpayers whose tax returns they personally prepared and signed. Furthermore, their authority is restricted to discussions before IRS customer service representatives, revenue agents, and similar frontline personnel. An Annual Filing Season Program participant cannot represent a taxpayer in an IRS appeals conference or handle collection matters.

Preparers with even fewer credentials have no standing before the IRS at all. A preparer who holds only an active Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) without completing the Annual Filing Season Program or holding a recognized professional credential has had no representation authority before the IRS since January 1, 2016. Such preparers cannot speak for a client during an audit or dispute, even if they prepared the return in question. A taxpayer evaluating representation options across different credentials can review the detailed [tax attorney vs CPA vs Enrolled Agent](/compare/tax-attorney-vs-cpa-vs-enrolled-agent/) comparison.

sections.heading: Form 2848 as the Official Authorization Mechanism
sections.body:
IRS [Form 2848](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-2848), titled Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, is the formal document that authorizes an eligible professional to represent a taxpayer before the IRS. Executing Form 2848 grants the designated representative two distinct legal powers: the authority to inspect and receive the taxpayer's confidential tax return information, and the authority to perform legal acts that the taxpayer could perform. Those legal acts include signing agreements, consents, and waivers related to the tax issues specified on the document. In addition to standard federal tax matters, Form 2848 covers Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) examinations.

Form 2848 is not a blanket grant of universal authority across a taxpayer's entire financial history. Part I of the form requires the taxpayer to identify the exact tax matters, the specific tax form numbers, and the precise years or accounting periods covered by the authorization. This structure creates an important operational boundary for representation. Because the authorization is strictly scoped to the listed matters and periods, a CPA authorized for an audit of one specific tax year has no standing to speak with the IRS regarding a different, unlisted year, even if the underlying accounting dispute is identical. When an examination expands to adjacent tax years, the taxpayer must submit a new or amended Form 2848 naming those additional periods before the CPA can take action on them.

Eligible representatives named on Form 2848 extend beyond CPAs and attorneys. The [Instructions for Form 2848](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i2848) list several categories of eligible representatives: CPAs, attorneys, Enrolled Agents, Enrolled Actuaries, Enrolled Retirement Plan Agents, corporate officers representing an organization, full-time employees, certain family members (spouse, parent, child, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, and corresponding step-relations), unenrolled return preparers for returns they prepared, and qualifying students or law graduates working in a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic (LITC) or Student Tax Clinic Program (STCP).

When completing Form 2848, the representative must complete Part II, known as the Declaration of Representative. In Part II, the CPA designates their professional qualification, provides their Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number, and attests to their current authorization to practice under Circular 230. The CAF number is a unique nine-digit identification number assigned by the IRS to track authorized representatives. It is distinct from a representative's Social Security number, Employer Identification Number, Preparer Tax Identification Number, or state license number.

sections.heading: Form 2848 vs Form 8821: Representation vs Information Authorization
sections.body:
Taxpayers frequently confuse Form 2848 with IRS [Form 8821](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8821), titled Tax Information Authorization. While both forms grant access to confidential tax data, their legal scope is entirely different. Form 8821 authorizes a designated appointee solely to inspect or receive confidential tax return information from the IRS. It provides visibility into transcripts, account records, and notices. However, Form 8821 does not grant any power of attorney. It does not authorize the recipient to speak on the taxpayer's behalf, advocate positions, answer examination questions, or negotiate settlements with the IRS.

Form 2848 includes all the disclosure access of Form 8821 but adds full representation rights. A representative named on Form 2848 can actively negotiate, respond to formal IRS proposals, sign waivers extending the statutory assessment period, and execute closing agreements on the listed tax matters. If a taxpayer only requires a third party to review account balances or inspect historical filings, Form 8821 satisfies that purpose without conferring legal agency. Whenever a professional must respond to an IRS examiner, handle collection inquiries, or argue disputed deductions before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, Form 2848 is mandatory.

sections.heading: How to File Form 2848
sections.body:
The IRS accepts Form 2848 through three administrative channels: online submission, fax, and postal mail. One filing option is the official online portal at [IRS.gov/Submit2848](https://www.irs.gov/submit2848). This online submission tool allows taxpayers and representatives to upload completed forms and supports electronic signatures.

Taxpayers and practitioners who do not use the online tool must submit the completed form by fax or postal mail. The correct fax number and mailing address depend directly on the taxpayer's geographic location, as detailed in the Instructions for Form 2848. The IRS instructions do not state a filing fee for processing Form 2848. There is no indicated agency fee to record or maintain the power of attorney on the IRS Centralized Authorization File system. A taxpayer evaluating resolution strategies while submitting authorization documents can review estimated procedural costs with a [tax resolution calculator](/tax-resolution/).

sections.heading: Scope and Boundaries of CPA IRS Representation
sections.body:
Once a valid Form 2848 is processed and recorded on the CAF system, a CPA can manage every aspect of the designated tax controversy directly with the IRS. The CPA can attend audit meetings, supply supporting books and records, submit legal and accounting memorandums, and challenge proposed adjustments. If the examining revenue agent issues an adverse finding, the CPA can formally file a protest and represent the taxpayer in settlement conferences before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. In collection matters, the CPA can negotiate installment agreements or submit documentation to resolve outstanding tax liabilities.

Representation rights before the administrative branches of the IRS do not automatically translate to authority in federal judicial forums. A CPA's unlimited representation rights are confined to the executive agency. For example, representation in the United States Tax Court requires separate admission under the court's own rules, as explained in the guide on [whether an Enrolled Agent can represent a taxpayer in Tax Court](/guides/can-an-enrolled-agent-represent-you-in-tax-court/). Similarly, representation rules vary across other representative types on Form 2848. For instance, the authorization for a qualifying student or law graduate under an LITC or STCP automatically expires 130 days after the taxpayer signs the form, after which the IRS purges that student representative from the system. This specific 130-day auto-expiration rule applies only to that student clinic category.

This guide provides general informational analysis of IRS practice standards and does not constitute formal legal or tax advice. A taxpayer facing an audit, collection notice, or proposed adjustment should evaluate their specific case with a licensed CPA, tax attorney, or Enrolled Agent.

faqs.question: Can a CPA represent a client before the IRS?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Treasury Circular 230, a Certified Public Accountant in good standing holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS. A CPA can represent a client on any tax matter, including audits, collection actions, and administrative appeals, regardless of who originally prepared the tax return.

faqs.question: Does a taxpayer need to file Form 2848 for a CPA to speak with the IRS on their behalf?
faqs.answer: Yes. The IRS requires a processed Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, before agency personnel can disclose confidential tax information to a CPA or recognize the CPA's legal authority to advocate, negotiate, or execute agreements on the taxpayer's behalf.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Form 2848 and Form 8821?
faqs.answer: Form 2848 authorizes a representative to both inspect confidential tax records and legally act or speak on the taxpayer's behalf before the IRS. Form 8821 only authorizes a designated party to inspect or receive confidential tax records, granting no power to represent, negotiate, or advocate.

faqs.question: What is a CAF number?
faqs.answer: A Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number is a unique nine-digit identification number assigned by the IRS to an authorized representative. It is used by the IRS to track third-party authorizations and is separate from a Social Security number, Employer Identification Number, or PTIN.

faqs.question: Can Form 2848 be filed online?
faqs.answer: Yes. Form 2848 can be submitted online through the IRS submission tool at IRS.gov/Submit2848, which supports electronic signatures. Filers can also transmit the form via fax or postal mail to specific IRS locations based on the taxpayer's state of residence.

faqs.question: Is there a fee to file Form 2848?
faqs.answer: The IRS instructions for Form 2848 do not state a filing fee. There is no indicated agency fee charged by the IRS to submit, process, or record the power of attorney authorization on the Centralized Authorization File system.
